chapter_theme: The king flies with the queen in the sky chariot the god's mantra supplies; Naravahanan is born and grows up with four companions, sees and unites with Madanamanjikai, who is carried off by the Vidyadhara Manasavegan, and Manasavegan's sister Vegavati, sent to break her firmness, falls in desire for the prince and takes Madanamanjikai's form.

cast.role: the king of Vatsa, whose queen is with child
Udayanan's queen (called தத்தை in these verses), who longs to travel the sky
the god who once showed Udayanan water and gave him a mantra to call him
Udayanan's minister, who recalls the god

a minister's son, companion of Naravahanan

242.reading: Because the king's sceptre runs justly over every quarter, skilled folk and common men bow to his feet, and Dattai, the queen in her garland, falls into a longing.
242.nuance: The word மயற்கை (longing, bewilderment) opens the next verse, where the longing is named as a wish to fly.
242.event: People marvel and bow at the just king's feet, and the queen Dattai falls into a longing.

243.reading: As the child grows in the queen's womb like a crescent, she is seized by a lack in her longing, to go in the sky; the king hears it, thinks it over and calls his ministers to ask.
243.event: The queen in pregnancy longs to travel the sky, and the king calls his ministers to ask what can be done.

244.reading: Urumannuva recalls to the king that once, when thirst overcame him on a hunt in the great hill forest, a god appeared and showed him water and ended his great distress.
244.nuance: Line 1 can be read as the king bidding Urumannuva speak, or as Urumannuva beginning; the sense of the recalled rescue is the same.
244.event: Urumannuva reminds the king how a god once appeared to the thirsty king in a hunt and showed him water.

245.reading: The god, when he left, gave a lasting mantra and said to think of it in any trouble; the king now thinks of it with care and the proud god arrives at once.
245.event: Udayanan calls to mind the mantra the god gave him, and the god comes.

246.reading: After many courtesies the god speaks to the king: in the days of prison, when the savaras closed in and harassed him, when he was parted from Vasavadatta, and when he killed his enemies...
246.nuance: The sentence is left unfinished here and is completed in the next verse: in none of these troubles did the king call on him.
246.event: The god begins to list the king's past dangers, prison, the savara attack, the parting from Vasavadatta and his killing of foes.

247.reading: The god says the king never once thought of him as a friend in those troubles and asks why he has remembered him on this strange day; the king answers that the queen has wished to go in the sky.
247.nuance: Lines 1 to 3 are the god's question and line 4 is the king's answer, given by the narrator in indirect speech. The god treats the bond as one that needs a call.
247.event: The god asks why the king calls on him now, and the king answers that the queen longs to travel the sky.

248.reading: The king explains that what they could do among themselves they have done, but the queen's travel in the sky cannot come about except through the god, and so he thought of him now; the god hears it well and tells the king to listen.
248.event: Udayanan tells the god why he called him, and the god bids him listen.

249.reading: The god tells the king of a god of the silver mountain who has come to dwell in the fragrant-haired woman's womb, whose delight makes her wander in thought; the king then mounts the jewelled chariot, and the mantra is given for flying like a bird.
249.nuance: Lines 1 and 2 are hard to read, and who gives the mantra in lines 3 to 4 is inferred from the story, since no one is named; the verse seems to trace the longing to the being in her womb.
249.event: The god explains the cause of the queen's longing and gives the king a mantra to make the chariot fly.

250.reading: The king and queen and their friends mount the victory chariot in order, rise into the sky, see the Himalaya in the north and then turn to the east.
250.event: Udayanan, the queen and friends fly the chariot north to the Himalaya and then east.

251.reading: They see the eastern hill of sunrise, go on to the south and the Podiyil hill, see the western mountain where sun and moon set, and having seen the good lands return to their pleasant city.
251.nuance: Lines 1 and 4 carry stray full stops inside words in the edition (கிரி.யும், புரி.ய).
251.event: The riders fly over the eastern, southern and western hills and return to their city.

252.reading: When the queen's longing has ended and they have entered the rich city, the planets all stand well, the prince is born, and the king, glad, opens the gold chamber and scatters wealth to all the people.
252.event: The prince is born under good planets, and the king opens his gold chamber and gives to all.

253.reading: The king names the child Naravahanan, and the four sons of his ministers have the names Gomukhan, Tarisakan, Nagadattan and Bhuti.
253.nuance: The line that gives the four names runs together across lines 3 and 4 (பாங்காந் தரிசக னாக தத்தன், குலமறி பூதி), so the exact form of the names is somewhat uncertain.
253.event: Udayanan names his son Naravahanan, and the four minister's sons are named.

254.reading: The four become his companions, share his ghee and milk, crawl in the wooden cradle and grow like the third-day moon; when childhood is past, they place him in the company of Vani.
254.nuance: Who is placed and who places him is not stated; பான்மொழி வாணி may be the goddess of learning or a teacher's name.
254.event: The prince and the four minister's sons grow up together and are placed with Vani for learning.

255.reading: The youth, who has taken all the sweetness of learning, looks to onlookers like Kama himself, and with his friends and army before and behind rides an elephant through the town's streets.
255.nuance: Line 1 is hard: ஞானநற் குமரி is read here as learning personified, but that is not certain, and line 2 is hard to parse.
255.event: Naravahanan, grown and learned, rides an elephant through the streets with his friends and army.

256.reading: As a cool breeze blows on Madanamanjikai, born of Kalingasenai, who plays with the ball in the decorated court, the king's son sees her.
256.event: Naravahanan sees Madanamanjikai playing ball in the court.

257.reading: The prince sees the garlanded girl and both are bewildered by the god of love's arrow; in the flower grove he unites with the slender-waisted girl at once, to their joy.
257.nuance: The verse names no wedding, no go-between and no family: sight and union come together. Whether there is a rite that is left out is not clear from the verse.
257.event: The prince and Madanamanjikai fall in love at the sight and unite in the flower grove.

258.reading: While the two sleep after their pleasure, the Vidyadhara king Manasavegan sees the radiant girl, takes her by his skill and enters his city on the silver mountain.
258.nuance: The abduction falls at the moment of rest after union, so the girl is taken before the lovers are fully known to the household.
258.event: Manasavegan carries off the sleeping Madanamanjikai to the silver mountain.

259.reading: When Manasavegan tells her his pain she keeps silent and holds her husband sweetly in mind; so he sends his slender-waisted sister Vegavati, to ruin the firmness she keeps.
259.nuance: Silence and remembering her husband are the whole of her defence; the verse calls her husband இன்னுயிர்க் கணவன், though no rite of marriage was told in the last verses.
259.event: Manasavegan woos her in vain, and sends Vegavati to break her steadfastness.

260.reading: Madanamanjikai, unmoved, says with love that her lord is like Indra himself; hearing the words of such a virtuous woman, Vegavati falls into a trance of feeling and comes out in the sky, and sees Naravahanan.
260.nuance: Who says what in lines 1 and 2 is hard to fix; the speech is taken here to be Madanamanjikai's, praising her husband, and Vegavati's trance is taken to follow from it.
260.event: Madanamanjikai praises her lord to Vegavati, who comes to the sky and sees Naravahanan.

261.reading: On seeing him Vegavati's desire grows and she stands in the dark sky, while the youth, stricken, searches the groves, the towers and the whole wood for the girl, and Vegavati comes down by guile.
261.nuance: The desire in line 1 is taken as Vegavati's, since she is the one who has just seen him, but the grammar does not fix it.
261.event: Vegavati, desiring Naravahanan, descends by a trick while he is searching everywhere for Madanamanjikai.

262.reading: Vegavati takes the shape of Madanamanjikai, doe-eyed, with a moon-like face, wearing the pleasing disguise with delight, and sits in a bower within the thicket.
262.event: Vegavati takes on Madanamanjikai's form and waits in a thicket pavilion.

links.note: The queen's longing named in 242 is given its object in 243.
links.teaches: The vague longing of 242 is shown to be a wish for flight in the sky, which sets the plot of the next verses in motion.

links.note: The mantra the god gave in the hunt is now used.
links.teaches: The god's rescue is not only a past kindness: it left a means to call him, so the gift becomes the tool for the present trouble.

links.note: In both epics a god gives a hero a spell to call on, and a later need brings him.
links.teaches: Both Jain epics let a god leave a gift of spells that later serves the hero, so the helping god is a recurring structure of the genre.

links.note: The Kural's friend clears distress at once; the god's help waits to be called.
links.teaches: The god's reproach shows a friend's help can be bound by the call, which limits the Kural's picture of friendship that acts in the moment of trouble.

gains.a: The god's ask-and-answer scene shows that friendship with a god runs on being remembered, and that the king neglected it until now.
gains.b: The couplet's friend who acts unasked gets a counterexample: help that needs a call, and stays silent through prison and war.

links.note: The cause of the queen's longing is given and the means of flight supplied.
links.teaches: The longing for the sky is explained as the doing of the being in her womb, so the flight is both a cure and a sign of the child's nature.

links.note: The birth closes the pregnancy that began with the longing for the sky.
links.teaches: The longing, met by the flight, is followed by an easy birth and gifts, so the god's help is shown to have ended the trouble as well as quieting it.
The ball-play scene is not an end in itself: the sight of her carries at once into union, which makes her loss in 258 sharper.

links.note: The Kural's bewildered first sight is here mutual and immediate.
links.teaches: The epic carries the Kural's bewilderment through to union within a single verse, with no doubt, no gossip and no delay, so the bewilderment is a path to union and not a state of suffering.

gains.a: The verse shows both lovers bewildered, and it leaves out the mourning and doubt that the Kural's chapter dwells on.
gains.b: The couplet's lone man, unsure whether she is goddess, peahen or woman, gets a case in which the sight is answered and the doubt never has time to arise.

links.note: The captor confines her and then tries to break her steadfastness; the Kural says only her own firmness guards a woman.
links.teaches: Here the confinement works as the couplet says it must: the captor holds her body, yet only her silence and thought of her husband stand in the way, so the guard is inside her.

gains.a: The abducted girl's silence and memory show what the guard inside a woman is made of in practice, which the epic otherwise leaves unnamed.
gains.b: The couplet's claim that confinement guards nothing gets a hard test: she is truly confined, in the house of a king who wants her.

links.note: The one sent to break another woman's firmness is overcome by desire herself.
links.teaches: The plan to ruin Madanamanjikai's steadfastness reverses: the agent of the attack is the one who loses control, which turns the test of one woman into the downfall of another.

links.note: Vegavati's trick in 261 is carried out as a disguise in 262.
links.teaches: The guile that was only named in 261 is shown as taking the very form of the woman Naravahanan is looking for, which turns his search into the means of her plan.

links.note: Desire breaks through the restraint of the one who was to be the tempter.
links.teaches: Vegavati was sent as the instrument of a plan, and she meets desire the Kural says does not stop to ask whether one is firm in restraint, which makes the plan itself the thing that fails.

gains.a: The verse shows desire overcoming the person of the plan, a case the couplet's general remark does not name.
gains.b: The couplet's general claim that love ignores restraint gets a case where it defeats an agent with an assigned task, not only a lover who is open to it.

source_issues: Verse 244 line 1: whether Urumannuva speaks or is bidden to speak is not clear.
Verse 249 lines 1 to 2: the grammar is hard and the speaker of the mantra is not named.
Verse 251 lines 1 and 4: stray full stops inside words (கிரி.யும், புரி.ய).
Verse 253 lines 3 to 4: the four names run together.
Verse 254 line 4 and verse 255 lines 1 to 2: hard to read.
Verse 260 lines 1 to 2: the speaker and the one addressed are not clear.
